Light, dark and the system's look as three commands of the registry, the same in every app of the suite (owner,
2026-11-23): the person chooses the scheme from the palette, and no app writes commands or theme code for it. The app
calls `useSchemeCommands` inside its `CommandsProvider` with its look (its theme, and the user's tone or own colours
when it has them) and the key of the browser's storage the choice is kept under. The three commands sit in a group of
their own («Look», `useWords().scheme`), each with its icon (R6) and a name that stands alone without the heading
(«Light theme»: a screen reader says the row, not the group); the one in use is checked. Choosing one puts the theme
in that scheme on the document's root at once (`applyTheme`) and keeps it. The pages and the tabs that keep the choice
under the same key follow it, and the system's choice, the default, follows `prefers-color-scheme` while the page is
open. A value kept that is not light, dark or the system's is the system's. The storage is the answer whenever it can
be read; only where the browser gives no storage at all does a choice hold in the page, until it is closed.
`applyKeptScheme`, called in the app's entry before React renders, puts the kept choice on the root as soon as that
script runs. On a server nothing reads the browser's storage: the choice is the system's, drawn light. After Imago's
`mountApp`, whose palette had the same commands.

types.name: SchemeState
types.doc: The choice, and the scheme drawn now (for the system's choice, the one the system says).

files.about:
A deck of cards decided one at a time, each to one of two sides: keep or skip, approve or refuse, now or later.
One card, one decision: nothing else on the screen asks for attention while a pile is sorted.
Three ways to decide, all the same decision: drag the card past a third of the way (or flick it) and let go; press
the left or right arrow with the card in focus; or press one of the two buttons under the deck, which are always
there and never move (R14), so nothing depends on a gesture. While the card is dragged far enough, the word of the
side it would go to shows on it: what letting go will do is said before it is done.
The deck keeps nothing: the app holds the cards (`items`, the first is on top) and takes the decided one out when
`onSwipe` tells it; to take a decision back it puts the card first again (an `Undo` in a notice, `Toasts`). A card
the app leaves in comes back to its place.
The card follows the finger at once (that is the gesture, not an animation); thrown, it leaves with a movement only
when motion is on (`animated`, or `MotionProvider`). The next card lies under the top one, still: the flat page has
no stack that zooms.

components.name: SwipeDeck
components.doc: A deck of cards decided one at a time, to the left or to the right.

props.name: items
props.doc: The cards still to decide; the first is on top. The app takes a card out when it is decided.

props.name: getKey
props.doc: What tells a card from the others.

props.name: getLabel
props.doc: The card's name for screen readers (its title).

props.name: children
props.doc: What a card shows: laid out with the toolkit's parts (`Heading`, `Text`, `DescriptionList`).

props.name: onSwipe
props.doc: A card was decided: the app takes it out of `items` (and offers Undo in a notice).

props.name: label
props.doc: The name of the deck for screen readers («Requests to review»).

props.name: leftLabel
props.doc: What each side means, in a word or two («Skip», «Keep»): the buttons under the deck, and the word on a dragged card.

props.name: leftIcon
props.doc: The icons of the two buttons. Default the two arrows.

props.name: empty
props.doc: What takes the deck's place when no card is left (an `Empty`). Absent: the toolkit's words.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: No card can be decided (while a decision is being saved).

props.name: animated
props.doc: The thrown card leaves with a movement. Absent: as `MotionProvider` says.

files.about:
The theme gallery: a compact picker of the app's themes, one tile each. A tile is drawn in its own theme, in the
scheme and tone the app shows now (`themeVariables` on the tile alone): its name on the theme's primary fill, then a
small sketch of a window (the sidebar with a chosen row, two rows, a button), so the person sees the theme before
choosing it. The tiles are one radio group: one Tab stop, the arrows, Home and End move and choose (`radioArrows`, as
the look settings' cards), and the chosen tile has the accent edge and a check in a dot (the choice is not shown by
the edge alone). An optional last tile, dashed, stands for a theme of the person's own: choosing it calls the app,
which opens its own editor; it is the chosen one when `selected` is null. Two columns, three from 352px of its own
width (a container query: it fits a narrow settings panel).

components.name: ThemeGallery
components.doc: A compact theme picker. Each tile samples its own surfaces in the active scheme and tone. A null selection marks the optional custom tile, whose editor belongs to the caller.

files.about:
Park UI (MIT) tree-view 102769c — recipe translated to Tailwind for @acaprino/sigrid (https://github.com/chakra-ui/park-ui/blob/102769c/packages/preset/src/recipes/tree-view.ts)
A tree of rows: things that hold other things (folders and files, sections and pages, any hierarchy), each a row with
its name, one of Sigrid's icons, a short fact and a count at its end, and the rows it holds under it, one level in.
Behaviour: Ark UI's TreeView. The rows are one Tab stop (the chosen row when it is in sight); Down and Up move, Right
opens a branch and then goes into it, Left closes it and then goes out to the branch that holds the row, Home and End
reach the first and the last row in sight, the first letters of a name reach it, `*` opens the branches beside the
row; Enter, Space or a press choose a row, and on a branch also open or close it. One row is chosen, never several.
The row that has the focus is the `treeitem` itself, with its level, whether it is open and whether it is chosen: on a
branch Ark's control is made the `treeitem`, and the rows it holds are its `group` (`aria-owns`). A closed branch's
rows are not in the page.
Branches whose children the app loads (`hasChildren` and `loadChildren`) load them when they are opened: the row says
«Loading» meanwhile and takes no second opening (Enter and Right do nothing on it), and if the load fails it says so
and stays closed, so opening it again tries again. The tree loads them itself, not through Ark, which would keep a
branch «loaded» for ever: children belong to the node object they were loaded for, and when the app gives another
object for that id (another project, the same folder read again), or none, they are dropped.
The filter (`query`, typed in the field of `search` or given by the app) keeps what `match` finds (by default: the name
holds the text) with all it holds, and the branches that lead to a find, opened. What the person opens or closes
meanwhile is theirs: when the filter is cleared their own branches come back, with those changes.
Form: Park's `tree-view` recipe on the toolkit's tokens: rows of the density's row height (44px with a finger), l2,
14px, one level in 20px (Park's 22px, on the 4px grid). At the start the chevron of the sidebar's groups (14px in a
16px slot, a quarter turn when open, turning only with `animated`), then the icon, the name, and at the end the fact
in 12px tabular figures and a `Count` (R5). The row's look is that of every list of things (`lib/rows.ts`, as
`ItemRow`): under the pointer a share of the selection tint; the chosen row has the whole tint, its ink and the short
accent bar at its start (R1), and its name in semibold. Not taken from Park: the chevron in the accent (R2: it is
chrome, in the muted ink), the semibold of the first level (semibold says «chosen»), the line that guides the eye
down a branch, the transitions.
What a row draws is memoised: a move of the focus paints Ark's own parts again (its context is new at each move), not
the icons, names and facts of every row.
It is not the graph: `GraphCanvas` and its tree mode draw things joined by lines; this is a list of nested rows, and
the two share no code.

props.name: aria-label
props.doc: Name of the tree for screen readers («Files»).

props.name: nodes
props.doc: The first level of the tree. Children loaded for a node stay while the app gives the same node object: build the nodes once (a constant, state, `useMemo`), and give a new object for a node whose children must be read again (another project, a refresh).

props.name: selected
props.doc: The chosen row, by its id, or null for none. With it the choice is the app's: pass the id `onSelect` gives.

props.name: defaultSelected
props.doc: The row chosen at first, when the choice is the tree's own.

props.name: onSelect
props.doc: The person chose a row (a press, Enter or Space): its id, and the node.

props.name: expanded
props.doc: The branches the person opened, by id. With it they are the app's: pass the list `onExpandedChange` gives. The branches the filter opens are not in it. A branch still to load stays closed until the person opens it.

props.name: defaultExpanded
props.doc: The branches open at first, when they are the tree's own.

props.name: onExpandedChange
props.doc: The person opened or closed a branch: the whole list of the branches they opened. A branch that loads joins it once its rows are here. Not called when the list did not change.

props.name: loadChildren
props.doc: Loads the rows of a branch with `hasChildren`, when it is first opened. A promise that fails leaves the branch closed, saying so; opening it again tries again. The signal says the tree no longer waits (the node changed or left, the tree left the page).

props.name: search
props.doc: A field above the rows that filters them (`query`).

props.name: searchLabel
props.doc: The name and placeholder of that field. Absent: the toolkit's words («Filter by name»).

props.name: query
props.doc: The text that filters the rows. With it the text is the app's: pass what `onQueryChange` gives. It filters with the tree's field (`search`) or without it, from a field of the app's (`ToolbarSearch`). Only spaces, or nothing: no filter.

props.name: defaultQuery
props.doc: The text the filter starts with, when it is the tree's own.

props.name: onQueryChange
props.doc: The text of the filter changed: typed in the tree's field, or cleared.

props.name: match
props.doc: Whether a node is found by the text, given as it is (`query`), only when it holds more than spaces. Absent: its name holds the text, whatever the case and the spaces at its ends. A node found shows with all it holds; a branch that leads to one shows with what it keeps, opened. Branches never loaded are not searched: to have them searched, give their children. An app counts the finds with the same function over its own nodes. A constant, or memoised: a new function filters again.

props.name: animated
props.doc: The chevron of a branch turns when it opens or closes, as the sidebar's groups (off by default, never with prefers-reduced-motion).

types.name: TreeNode
types.doc: A thing of the tree: a row, and the rows it holds.

fields.name: id
fields.doc: Names the thing among all the others of the tree (a path, a key): the choice and the open branches are ids.

fields.name: name
fields.doc: What the row says; the filter by default and the first letters typed look for it.

fields.name: icon
fields.doc: A meaning of Sigrid's icons (`folder`, `file`…); a name Sigrid does not draw is an empty slot. In a tree where some rows have one, a row without keeps an empty slot (R6).

fields.name: openIcon
fields.doc: The icon of a branch while it is open (`folderOpen` for a `folder`). Absent: `icon`, open or closed.

fields.name: meta
fields.doc: A short fact at the end of the row, in tabular figures: a size, a date.

fields.name: count
fields.doc: How many things the node holds or waits on (changed, unread): a `Count` at the end of the row, after `meta`. Zero shows nothing.

fields.name: children
fields.doc: The rows it holds. With an array (even empty) the row is a branch, which opens and closes.

fields.name: hasChildren
fields.doc: It holds rows the app loads when the branch is opened (`loadChildren`), until then unknown. Read only without `children`; without `loadChildren` the branch holds nothing.

files.about:
A table of data, ready to use: columns that sort when their heading is pressed, one row that can be chosen, and,
for thousands of rows, only the ones in sight in the page. The behaviour is TanStack's (`@tanstack/react-table` for
the columns and the sorting, `@tanstack/react-virtual` for the rows in sight: npm dependencies, pinned, see
THIRD_PARTY.md); the form is the toolkit's `Table` parts. It lives in its own entry of the package (`./table`), so
an app without a table does not load either library.
- A column says its heading, what a cell shows, and the value it sorts by. Without that value the heading is a
  word and not a button. A press sorts up, a second down, a third puts the rows back as they were given. The
  heading says how it is sorted with `aria-sort`, and with an arrow for the eye.
- With `onRowPress` a row is pressed with the pointer or with Enter and Space; the arrows, Home and End move among
  the rows, which are one Tab stop, as in a list: the row that had the focus last, or the chosen one, or the first
  in sight. A press on a control inside a cell (a button, a link, a field) is that control's and not the row's.
  The chosen row (`current`) has the selection tint (R1).
- With `virtual` the box needs a height (`className="h-96"`): the rows outside it are not in the page, two spacer
  rows keep the scrollbar honest, and each row is measured as it is drawn, so any density and a finger's 44px hold.
  Home and End go to the first and the last row of the data. A row scrolled far out of sight is no longer in the
  page, and the focus it had goes with it: Tab comes back to a row in sight.
- `columns` is best made once (outside the component, or with `useMemo`): a new array at every paint sorts the
  rows again at every paint.
An app that needs more of a table (filters, pinned columns, groups) drives TanStack Table itself and draws it with
`Table`, `TableRow` and `TableCell`: this component is the common case, not a wall around the library.

props.name: aria-label
props.doc: The name of the table for screen readers («Files»).

props.name: rowId
props.doc: What tells a row from the others, and stays the same when the rows are sorted.

props.name: sort
props.doc: The sorting, when the app keeps it; otherwise the table keeps its own, starting from `defaultSort`.

props.name: current
props.doc: The id of the row chosen: the one shown in the details.

props.name: onRowPress
props.doc: With it, a row is pressed: with the pointer, or with Enter and Space.

props.name: virtual
props.doc: Only the rows in sight are in the page: for thousands of rows. The box needs a height (`className`).

props.name: empty
props.doc: In place of the rows when there are none. Absent: the toolkit's words («Nothing to show»).

props.name: className
props.doc: Classes of the box that scrolls: its height.

fields.name: header
fields.doc: The heading of the column.

fields.name: cell
fields.doc: What a cell of the column shows.

fields.name: sortValue
fields.type: ((row: Row) => string | number | Date | null | undefined)
fields.doc: The value the column sorts by: a text, a number, a date. Without it the column does not sort.

fields.name: align
fields.doc: `end`: a column of numbers, set at the end in tabular figures.

fields.name: className
fields.doc: Classes for the heading and the cells of the column: its width (`w-24`), no wrapping.

types.name: DataSort
types.doc: The column the rows are sorted by, and the direction. Null: as they were given.

files.about:
A long list of which only the rows in sight are in the page: ten thousand messages cost what thirty do. The rows
are the toolkit's own (`ItemRow`, or any `<li>`); this part is the box that scrolls and the choice of which rows to
draw, on TanStack Virtual (`@tanstack/react-virtual`, an npm dependency, pinned: THIRD_PARTY.md). It has its own
entry of the package (`./virtual`), so an app with short lists does not load the library.
- The rows of a list are all as tall as each other, so one of them is measured as it is drawn and the rest follow:
  any density holds, and so do the 44px of a finger. `estimateSize` is only where the first paint starts from.
- The room of the rows not drawn is kept as padding, so the scrollbar is the one of the whole list.
- For screen readers it is a list that says how many items it holds and where each one is (`aria-setsize`,
  `aria-posinset`): what is not drawn is still counted.
The box needs a height: `fill` makes it as tall as the region that holds it (the content, a pane of `ContentSplit`),
as `Empty fill` and `Page fit` are, so an app writes no class for it; beside other parts in a `Column fill` it takes
what they leave. `pad` is the room inside the box, around the rows, a step of the scale.

props.name: aria-label
props.doc: Name of the list for screen readers («Messages»).

props.name: count
props.doc: How many rows the list holds.

props.name: children
props.doc: The row at a place, counted from 0: an `ItemRow`, or any `<li>`. One element for each place, never none.

props.name: rowKey
props.doc: What tells the row at a place from the others, where the rows move: its id. Absent: its place.

props.name: estimateSize
props.doc: The height of a row in px before one is measured. Default 44.

props.name: overscan
props.doc: How many rows are drawn beyond the ones in sight, on each side. Default 8.

props.name: fill
props.doc: As tall as the region that holds it, which gives it its height (the content of the frame, a pane): the box scrolls, not the region.

props.name: pad
props.doc: The room inside the box, around the rows: 4, 8, 12, 16 or 24px. Absent: none.

props.name: className
props.doc: Classes of the box that scrolls: its height, where it is not `fill`.

files.about:
A list the user puts in order: each row has a handle that moves it, with the pointer, a finger or the keyboard. The
behaviour is dnd-kit's (`@dnd-kit/core` and `@dnd-kit/sortable`, npm dependencies, pinned: THIRD_PARTY.md); the form
is the toolkit's. It has its own entry of the package (`./reorder`), so an app with no such list does not load it.
- The handle is the only thing that drags: the rest of the row keeps its presses, its fields and its text.
  With the keyboard: Space takes the row, the arrows move it, Space puts it down, Escape puts it back. Screen
  readers hear where it is at each step, in the app's words (`words.reorder`). While a row is taken, Escape is
  the list's: a dialog or a sheet the list is in stays open.
- The row taken is raised on the sheet colour with the `float` elevation and no border (R4), and follows the pointer
  up and down only. The others make room for it: at once, or sliding in 200ms where the app has motion on
  (`animated`, or `MotionProvider`), never with reduced motion.
- The list is the app's: `onReorder` gives the new order and the app keeps it. Nothing is kept here.

props.name: aria-label
props.doc: Name of the list for screen readers («Columns»).

props.name: itemId
props.doc: What tells an item from the others.

props.name: itemName
props.doc: The name of an item: of its handle («Move Inbox»), and what screen readers hear while it moves.

props.name: onReorder
props.type: (items: Item[], move: { from: number; to: number; }) => void
props.doc: The new order, and the place the item left and the one it took, counted from 0.

props.name: children
props.doc: What a row shows beside its handle.

props.name: animated
props.doc: The rows slide to make room (off by default, never with prefers-reduced-motion).

files.about:
A field for text with a little form: bold, italic and underlined words, two kinds of list, a quote. The editing is
TipTap's (`@tiptap/react` and its starter kit, on ProseMirror: npm dependencies, pinned, see THIRD_PARTY.md); the
form is the toolkit's: the border and the focus ring of a field, and above the text the toolkit's own `Toolbar`
with Sigrid's icons (R6). It has its own entry of the package (`./rich-text`): TipTap is the
heaviest thing the toolkit rests on, and an app that writes no formatted text does not load it.
- What the row of buttons offers is all the field does: headings, code, links and rules are switched off, so a
  paste or a shortcut cannot bring in what the user has no button to take away. The value holds what was written
  and nothing else: no empty paragraph is kept after a list (Enter twice leaves a list or a quote).
- A button that is on (the caret is in bold text) says so with the selection tint, as any switch of a toolbar.
- The value is HTML, the app's to keep: `onChange` gives it at every change. A value that comes from outside (a
  draft opened) replaces the text and is not a step of the undo: Ctrl+Z never brings the other draft back. The
  field's own changes never loop back, also when the app hands them back late (a store, a round trip): a value
  the field itself gave a moment ago is not taken for a new one.
- It takes what a `FormField` gives its control (`id`, `aria-describedby`, `aria-invalid`, `required`). A `<label>`
  names only the browser's own fields, so the text finds the label that points at its `id`, takes its name from it
  (`aria-labelledby`) and takes the focus when the label is pressed, as an input does.
- Text is 16px below 860px, so a phone does not zoom, and 14px above.

props.name: value
props.doc: The text, as HTML.

props.name: aria-label
props.doc: The name of the field for screen readers, where no label names it.

props.name: required
props.doc: Said to screen readers; whether an empty text is accepted is the app's to check.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: The text cannot be changed: half opacity, no buttons.

props.name: className
props.doc: Classes of the box around the buttons and the text: the least height of the text is its own (`min-h-24`).

files.about:
A canvas for a graph of things and what joins them (tasks and what they wait for, the parts of a project, notes
that lead to other notes, the calls between the parts of a program): the user moves over it, looks at one thing and
what is joined to it, opens and closes what hangs from a thing and, where the app lets them, draws: adds a thing,
joins two, takes one away. The canvas, its pan and zoom, the lines and the joining by hand are React Flow's
(`@xyflow/react`), the places of the things are dagre's (`@dagrejs/dagre`): npm dependencies, pinned, see
THIRD_PARTY.md. The form is the toolkit's. It has its own entry of the package (`./graph`) and its own stylesheet
(`./graph.css`), so an app without a graph loads neither.
- The graph is laid out by itself, in ranks: from the start to the end of the line (`direction="right"`) or from
  the head to the foot (`"down"`). The user does not place things by hand, so nothing can be lost off the canvas.
- Or the app lays it out, with a layout engine of its own (ELK in a worker) or by hand: a thing with an `x` and a
  `y` is drawn there, a line with `points` follows that route, and nothing is laid out here. All or nothing: the app's places are read only when every thing it passes has one;
  when one has none (a thing just added with the plus) dagre places them all again, until the app places it. A
  thing's `width` and `height` are its size in both cases (dagre lays out with them); without them it is 208px
  wide and 44px tall, 56px with a second line.
- After a new layout of the app's (a new `layoutKey`) the view is fitted to the whole graph again; a draw on the
  same key (another choice, new flags, the same places) keeps the view where the user moved it, and so does a change
  of the box's size.
- A thing is a raised surface with a shadow and no border (R4): an icon or a dot of its colour (R10), a name, a
  line under it, and on a thing outside what the graph is about (`external`) the word «external», 12px in the muted
  ink, never a dashed border; the name keeps some room and the word gives way first (the word, not the icon of that
  name, which leaves the app: `icons.tsx`). The chosen one has the selection
  tint (R1), or each of the several the app marks when it draws one of its things in several places; what is joined
  to them stays as it is and the rest is dimmed, so the eye finds the neighbourhood. Of the several, one is the
  choice: the first in the order of the things, which holds the Tab stop and is the one screen readers hear chosen;
  the others say in their description that they are chosen with it. The app shows the details of the chosen thing
  where it likes (the `Inspector` of the frame).
- Two ways to read the lines (`model`). In the tree mode, the default, a line says that a thing hangs from another:
  - A thing with others hanging from it has an arrow: closed, it says how many it hides, and the graph is laid out
    again without them. What can be reached another way stays in sight.
  - The keyboard is the one of a tree, and the things are one Tab stop: Down and Up go through what is in sight,
    Right opens or goes to the first thing that hangs, Left closes or goes back to what it hangs from, Home and End
    reach the ends, Enter chooses. Screen readers hear a tree: the name of a thing, its level, whether it is open,
    how many it hides.
- In the graph mode (`model="graph"`) a line is a relation (a call, an import, data that flows), not «hangs from»:
  - Nothing closes: every thing is in sight and none has an arrow. Opening a thing is the app's (going into it,
    showing what it holds), and only for the things it says it opens: a thing with an `openLabel` («Open Orders»)
    has a › button of that name, and a double press on it or its › calls `onOpen` with its id. Without `onOpen`,
    or on a thing without `openLabel`, there is no › and nothing opens. A thing that holds others the app keeps out
    of sight (a group it has not opened) says how many (`hiddenCount`), at its end as a closed thing of the tree does,
    and in its name.
  - The things are one Tab stop, and the › of the one that has it is the next. Along the ranks the arrows follow the
    lines: with `direction="right"` Right goes to what the thing's first line leads to and Left back to what its
    first line comes from, while Down and Up go through the things in the order the app gave them; downwards the
    axes swap. Home and End reach the first and the last thing of that order, Enter chooses. From the › the arrows,
    Home and End move as from its thing. Screen readers hear a group called a graph, of buttons named by their name
    and second line, described by where their lines lead and come from, the chosen one `aria-current`.
- In both modes + (or =, the same key without Shift), − and 0 zoom in, out and fit the whole graph, as the buttons
  at the head of the canvas do, and with `editable` Delete takes the thing away.
- Two kinds of line. A `child` line (the default) is the one each mode reads as above: in the tree mode these lines
  alone make the tree, what opens and closes, what a closed thing hides, the ranks and the keys. A `link` line joins
  two things without any of that (one waits for the other, one refers to the other, the two never go together) and
  is drawn only while both ends are in sight. A line may have words on it, a dash (`dashed`, `dotted`), a tone of the
  theme (`accent`, `warning`, `destructive`) and an arrowhead (a `link` has one unless it goes both ways): what a
  kind of line means is said by its dash and its words, never by its colour alone. Screen readers hear a thing's
  `link` lines in its description, with their words and the thing at the other end; the lines are not read twice.
  The words may be drawn only while one of the two things is chosen or has the focus, or while the line is the
  path's (`labelShown: 'chosen'`), and are heard always.
  An edge with an `id` is a line of its own: two between the same two things are two lines, each with its words. An
  edge without one is one line with its exact copies (the same ends, kind, words, dash, tone and arrowhead, and no
  route), and taking that line away takes them all; edges without ids that differ in any of those are lines of
  their own, numbered after their ends. Without the app's routes, two lines or more between the same two things are
  drawn side by side (a line type of the canvas's, `apart`), so the lines and their words do not lie on each
  other; with the routes each follows its own.
- With `steps` the app numbers a path through the graph (the steps of a plan, the answer to a question): each
  thing on it has the selection tint and its numbers in small dots and in its name, one line between two of them
  (the first in the order of the edges) is the path's, in the accent or in a tone of its own and thicker, what is
  neither on the path nor joined to it is dimmed, and what hides a thing of the path opens.
- The view is fitted at the first paint (on the path, when there is one), again whenever the box changes size, and
  with the button or the key: never smaller than a name can be read (`minFitZoom`, about 11px names). With a
  `layoutKey`, a view the user moved is not fitted again when the box changes size: it stays, panned only by what
  brings the chosen thing back into it. A graph too
  large for that starts at its top left, and the edges of the view fall between things wherever the layout leaves
  a gap between the floor and 1.5 (a dense graph in a small box may still have one cut). The app
  moves the view through a `ref`: `focus` (onto some things, opening what hides them), `fit`, `zoomTo`.
- With `search` a field finds things by name; the others are dimmed, and Enter goes to the first one found,
  opening what hides it.
- The box is 384px tall, or with `fill` as tall as the region that holds it (the content of the frame, a pane, the
  body of a `Page fit`, a `Column fill`), as `VirtualList fill` is: an app writes no class for it. Beside other parts
  in a pile (a row of filters above it, its key under it) it takes what they leave, and gives way when the region
  does; the view is fitted again. Never under 224px (232px with a finger): the field and the small map, one over the
  other at the start, are both whole (`FILL`). In less than that the region scrolls, and the canvas covers nothing
  that follows it (`Column fill`); in a region with no height of its own (a plain `Column`, a page that grows with
  what it holds) the box is that tall.
- With `editable` a thing shows its handles: drag from one to another thing to join them, press the plus on the
  chosen thing (the first of several, alone) to hang a new one from it (in the graph mode, to add one after it).
  Every change is asked of the app with `onChange`, which keeps the graph (and its undo, R12): nothing is kept here
  but what is open and where the view is.
The cost is the layout, done again when the graph changes or a thing opens or closes: about 30ms for 200 things in
sight, 200ms for a thousand, most of a second for three thousand (measured). In the tree mode a larger graph starts
with its branches closed (`defaultCollapsed`); in the graph mode every thing is in sight, so the whole graph is laid
out at every change of the nodes, the edges or the direction (choosing a thing or moving the focus lays out
nothing). With the app's places nothing is laid out here. Moving the view costs little: only what is in it is drawn.
Nothing moves by itself: the layout and the view jump to their new places, with or without animations, so reduced
motion is always honoured. The name of React Flow stays at the foot of the canvas, as its makers ask of whoever does
not pay for it.

components.name: GraphCanvas
components.doc: The canvas with the store the library needs around it.

props.name: aria-label
props.doc: The name of the graph for screen readers («Dependencies»).

props.name: model
props.doc: How the lines are read. `tree` (the default): a thing hangs from another, so a thing with others hanging from it opens and closes, and the keys and the roles are a tree's. `graph`: a line is a relation (a call, an import, data), every thing stays in sight with nothing that closes, the arrows follow the lines, and opening is the app's (`onOpen`).

props.name: direction
props.doc: The ranks go from the start of the line to its end, or from the head to the foot. Default `right`.

props.name: layoutKey
props.doc: The name of the layout the places come from, as the app tells one layout from another (the direction, the things and the lines it laid out). When it changes the view fits the whole graph again, once the new places are drawn; while it stays, a new draw (another choice, new flags, the same places) keeps the view where the user moved it. Pass the new key with the new places. A change of the box's size keeps a view the user moved, with the chosen thing still in it, and fits again one nobody moved. Without a key the view is fitted at the first paint and at every change of size.

props.name: selected
props.doc: The id of the thing chosen: the one whose details the app shows. Or several ids, when the app draws one of its things as several (an entity in each place it is): each has the selection tint and what is joined to it stays. One of them is the choice: the first in the order of the things, which holds the Tab stop, is the one screen readers hear chosen (`aria-selected` in the tree, `aria-current` in the graph mode) and, with `editable`, has the plus; the others say in their description that they are chosen with it (`graph.chosenToo`). The user still chooses one (`onSelect`).

props.name: onOpen
props.doc: In the graph mode, the app opens a thing (goes into it, shows what it holds): asked by a double press on a thing with an `openLabel` or by its › button. Without it nothing opens.

props.name: steps
props.doc: A path the app numbers through the graph: the id of each thing on it and its step numbers (a thing may be several steps). Each has the selection tint and its numbers; of the lines between two of them, the first in the order of the edges is the path's (the accent, or the line's own `tone`, thicker), so an app that wants another one there gives it first; what is neither on it nor joined to it is dimmed. When the things on it change, what hides one of them opens (through `onCollapsedChange` when the app keeps what is closed); the first view is on them.

props.name: collapsed
props.doc: In the tree mode, the ids of the things that are closed, when the app keeps them; otherwise the canvas keeps its own, from `defaultCollapsed`.

props.name: minFitZoom
props.doc: The smallest scale the view is fitted at (the first view, a change of size, the button, `fit`, `focus`): below it a name could not be read, so a graph too large starts at its top left instead. Default 0.8, names of about 11px; 0 fits the whole graph whatever its size, down to the smallest zoom (0.2). The user can still zoom out by hand.

props.name: search
props.doc: A field that finds things by name.

props.name: minimap
props.doc: A small map of the whole graph in a corner.

props.name: editable
props.doc: The user can hang a new thing, join two and take one away. Each change is asked for with `onChange`.

props.name: onChange
props.doc: The graph after a change, and the change: the app keeps the graph.

props.name: ref
props.doc: What the app can do to the view: `focus`, `fit`, `zoomTo`.

props.name: fill
props.doc: As tall as the region that holds it, which gives it its height (the content of the frame, a pane, the body of a `Page fit`, a `Column fill`): it takes what the parts beside it leave and gives way with it, never under 224px (232px with a finger), where the field and the small map are both whole. In a plain `Column`, which has no height to give, it is that tall and no more. Absent: 384px.

props.name: className
props.doc: Classes of the box: its height, where it is neither 384px nor `fill`.

types.name: GraphCanvasHandle
types.doc: What the app can do to the view, through the canvas's `ref`. The view jumps: nothing moves by itself.

fields.name: focus
fields.type: (ids: readonly string[], options?: { padding?: number | undefined; }) => void
fields.doc: Brings these things into the view, as large as fits and never smaller than `minFitZoom`, opening what hides them. The keyboard focus stays where it is. `padding`: px around them (default 24).

fields.name: fit
fields.doc: The whole graph in the view, as the button does: never smaller than `minFitZoom`, from the top left when it is too large for that.

fields.name: zoomTo
fields.doc: The scale of the view (1 is the things' own size), about the middle of the view.

types.name: GraphChange
types.doc: What the user did to the graph: a thing hung from another, two things joined, things and joins taken away.

types.name: GraphEdge
types.doc: What joins two things: by default, in the tree mode `to` hangs from `from`; in the graph mode the line goes from `from` to `to`.

fields.name: id
fields.doc: The app's name for the line, also React Flow's. An edge with an `id` is always a line of its own, so two between the same two things (a call, and data that flows the same way) are two lines, each with its words. Without one the line is named by its two ends, and a second one with the same ends by a number after them; an exact copy of an edge without an `id` (the same ends, `kind`, `label`, `labelShown`, `style`, `tone` and `directed`, and no `points`) is the same line, and taking that line away takes every copy.

fields.name: kind
fields.doc: `child` (the default): the line of the mode. In the tree mode `to` hangs from `from`, and these lines alone make the tree: what opens and closes, what a closed thing hides, the ranks of the layout, the keys. `link`: a line between two things that changes none of that (one waits for the other, refers to it, never goes with it), and in either mode no rank. Any other value is taken as `child`.

fields.name: label
fields.doc: Words on the line, in its middle. Screen readers hear them too, in the description of the two things.

fields.name: labelShown
fields.doc: When the words are drawn: `always` (the default), or `chosen`, only while one of the two things is chosen or has the keyboard focus, or while the line is the one of the path (`steps`) between its two things. Screen readers hear them in both cases.

fields.name: style
fields.doc: The dash of the line. What a kind of line means is said by its dash and its words, never by its colour alone. Default `solid`.

fields.name: tone
fields.doc: The colour of the line, among the theme's (each keeps 3:1 on the canvas): `accent` is also thicker. Default the muted ink. Kept on the path (`steps`), which takes the accent only on a line without a tone of its own.

fields.name: directed
fields.doc: An arrowhead at `to`. Default: a `link` has one, a `child` has none (its rank says which way it goes). `false` for a relation that goes both ways.

fields.name: points
fields.type: readonly { x: number; y: number; }[] | null
fields.doc: The route of the line when the app placed the things: its points from start to end, in px (a layout's start point, bends and end point). Read only with the app's places; without it, or with fewer than two points, the line goes from one side of a thing to the facing side of the other.

fields.name: label
fields.doc: The name of the thing: one line, cut with an ellipsis.

fields.name: detail
fields.doc: A second line under the name: a state, a date, a person.

fields.name: icon
fields.doc: One of Sigrid's icons before the name.

fields.name: color
fields.doc: The colour the user gave the thing (`#rrggbb`): an 8px dot before the name (R10).

fields.name: openLabel
fields.doc: In the graph mode, the name of the action that opens the thing and of its › button («Open Orders»): only a thing with it opens (its ›, a double press), and only when `onOpen` is given. The tree mode does not read it.

fields.name: external
fields.doc: The thing is outside what the graph is about (another's service, a library): the word «external» after its name, 12px in the muted ink (`graph.external`), also in its name for screen readers. Never a dashed border (R4). In a narrow box the name keeps some room and the word is cut first. It is a word and draws no icon: `icon` says what the thing is (`globe` for the web), and the icon `external` is for a press that leaves the app.

fields.name: hiddenCount
fields.doc: In the graph mode, how many things the app keeps out of sight inside this one (a group it has not opened): a count at its end, as a closed thing of the tree mode shows it, and in its name («Orders, hides 12», the word `graph.hides`). Read when above 0. The tree mode counts what a closed thing hides by itself and does not read it.

fields.name: x
fields.doc: Where the app placed the thing, when it lays the graph out itself (a layout engine of its own, by hand): the top left corner of its box, in px. Read only when every thing has an `x` and a `y`; otherwise the canvas places them all.

fields.name: width
fields.doc: The width and the height of its box in px, also when the canvas places it. Default 208 wide, 44 tall or 56 with a second line.

files.about:
The key of a graph's lines, under a `GraphCanvas`: each kind of line the app draws (its dash and its tone, as a
`GraphEdge` takes them), its word and, when the app gives it, how many there are (a `Count`, R5). Each sample is
drawn by the same definitions the canvas draws its lines with (`graph-lines.ts`, and one rule of graph.css), so a
change to a line changes its key. What a kind of line means is said by its word, never by its colour alone. A list
named by the app for screen readers, which hide the samples; a row that wraps on a narrow window. It keys the lines
only, not the things.

components.name: GraphLegend
components.doc: The key of a graph's lines: a sample of each kind, its word and its count, in a row that wraps. Nothing to key, nothing drawn.

props.name: entries
props.doc: The kinds of line, in the order given.

props.name: aria-label
props.doc: The name of the list for screen readers («Kinds of line»).

types.name: GraphLegendEntry
types.doc: One kind of line in the key.

fields.name: style
fields.doc: The dash of the line, as a `GraphEdge` takes it. Default `solid`.

fields.name: tone
fields.doc: The colour of the line, as a `GraphEdge` takes it. Default the muted ink.

fields.name: label
fields.doc: What a line of this kind means («calls», «waits for»): always written, so the colour is never alone.

fields.name: count
fields.doc: How many lines of this kind the graph has: a `Count` after the word, which screen readers hear with the word («12 calls»). Zero, or none, shows nothing.

files.about:
The calls the `./tauri` entry makes to a Tauri window, and the one place that loads Tauri's API. Each part of the
entry takes an `api` to call instead (a test passes a fake window, webview, `invoke` or `listen`); what it leaves out
is `tauriApi`, which imports `@tauri-apps/api` only inside its functions, the first time one is called. So a page in
a browser that imports the entry loads nothing of Tauri. The types are the entry's own: they name no type of
`@tauri-apps/api`, and `tauriApi` checks that Tauri's window and webview fit them.

types.name: TauriApi
types.doc: What the entry calls in Tauri.

fields.name: invoke
fields.doc: A command of the app's native side.

fields.name: listen
fields.type: <T>(event: string, handler: (event: { payload: T; }) => void) => Promise<Unlisten>
fields.doc: An event the native side sends.

types.name: TauriWebview
types.doc: The webview as the entry calls it: what `getCurrentWebview()` gives, or a fake one.

types.name: TauriWindow
types.doc: The window as the entry calls it: what `getCurrentWindow()` gives, or a fake one.

fields.name: onResized
fields.doc: Calls `handler` at each change of the window's size, until the returned function is called.

files.about:
Where the page runs, and the mark of the bar that moves the window. Both are plain reading: nothing of Tauri is
called or loaded, so they work in a browser and on a server too.
- A page in a Tauri window finds `__TAURI_INTERNALS__` on its window; a page in a browser does not.
- A window of its own is Tauri on a computer: its decorations are off, and the app draws the bar and its three
  buttons (`TitleBar` with `WindowControls`). On a phone the system draws its own.
- `DRAG_REGION` goes to `TitleBar`'s `dragProps`: Tauri moves the window from a press on an element that carries
  it, and maximizes it with a double press. It counts only on the element under the pointer, which is why the bar
  hands it to its toolbar, its title and its spacers.

types.name: TauriHost
types.doc: Where the page runs.

fields.name: native
fields.doc: In a Tauri window.

fields.name: mobile
fields.doc: On a phone or a tablet, in Tauri or in a browser.

fields.name: ownWindow
fields.doc: In a window of its own on a computer (Tauri, not on a phone): the app draws the window's bar and buttons.

files.about:
The permissions of Tauri 2 the entry's calls need, for the app's capability file (`src-tauri/capabilities/*.json`).
The plain skeleton of an app grants `core:default`: it holds what only reads (whether the window is maximized, the
double press that maximizes from the bar) and listening to events, but not the calls that change the window. The
identifiers are those of Tauri's core permissions (https://v2.tauri.app/reference/acl/core-permissions/); a
permission already in `core:default` is listed too, for a capability that does not grant it.
A command of the app's own (Snap Layouts, a window theme through a command) needs no core permission: Tauri allows
the app's commands to all its windows, unless the app narrows them with `AppManifest::commands` in its `build.rs`.

Snap Layouts on Windows 11, for a native side that offers them: opt-in, with the names the app's shell uses.
Windows opens its layouts from the system's own maximize button. A window without a frame has none, so a shell
can lay the system's hit area over the page's maximize button; then the pointer never reaches the page's button,
and the shell sends back its hover and press. This file does the page's half:
- it sends the button's rectangle to the app's command (`command`), in physical pixels (the page's pixels times
  `devicePixelRatio`, rounded) as `{ x, y, width, height }`, when it changes, again at each resize of the window
  (maximized, the shell places its area again) and after a change of zoom; a send that fails is sent again at the
  next change. When the button goes away a rectangle of zero size is sent, so the shell takes its area away;
- it listens to the app's event (`event`), whose payload is `{ hover, pressed }`, and gives `maximizeState`.
`useSnapLayouts` gives `maximizeRef` and `maximizeState`, the two props of `WindowControls` for it. The plain
skeleton of a Tauri app has no such command: without one, an app does not use this.

types.name: CaptionRect
types.doc: A rectangle in physical pixels.

fields.name: command
fields.doc: The app's command that takes the maximize button's rectangle (Imago's is `window_caption_maximize`).

fields.name: event
fields.doc: The app's event with `{ hover, pressed }` of that button (Imago's is `caption-maximize`).

fields.name: onError
fields.doc: Where a refused or failed call goes: `snapLayouts` for the command, `listen` for the event.

fields.name: enabled
fields.doc: Default: in a window of its own (`readHost().ownWindow`), or when `api` is given.

fields.name: api
fields.doc: What to call instead of Tauri's API (a fake `invoke` and `listen` in a test).

types.name: SnapLayoutsWiring
types.doc: The props of `WindowControls` for Snap Layouts.

files.about:
The three buttons of a window of its own, wired to the Tauri window: what `useWindowControls` gives is the props of
the toolkit's `WindowControls`, so an app writes `<WindowControls {...useWindowControls({ onError })} />`.
Whether the window is maximized is read at once and again at each change of its size; when several answers are on
their way (a window resized fast) only the last one asked is shown. A refused or failed call goes to `onError`, never
into an unhandled rejection. The listening stops on unmount, also when Tauri answers after it.

fields.name: onError
fields.doc: Where a refused or failed call goes. Without it a failure is dropped, never thrown.

fields.name: enabled
fields.doc: Default: in a window of its own (`readHost().ownWindow`), or when `api` is given. Off, the buttons do nothing.

fields.name: api
fields.doc: What to call instead of Tauri's API (a fake window in a test).

types.name: WindowControlsWiring
types.doc: The props of `WindowControls`, wired to the window.

files.about:
The theme of the window, opt-in: the scheme the page draws (`light` or `dark`) told to the window, so that what the
system draws around and behind the page (the frame on a computer that keeps one, a backdrop) matches it. It goes
through the window's `setTheme`, or, when the app names a command of its own, to that command with
`{ theme: 'light' | 'dark' }` (`args` gives other arguments). It is sent when the scheme changes, not at each draw;
a send that fails goes to `onError` and the next change tries again.

fields.name: command
fields.doc: The app's command that takes the theme. Without it, the window's own `setTheme`.

fields.name: args
fields.doc: The arguments of `command` for a scheme. Default `{ theme: scheme }`.

fields.name: onError
fields.doc: Where a refused or failed send goes, as `setTheme`.

fields.name: enabled
fields.doc: Default: in a window of its own (`readHost().ownWindow`), or when `api` is given.

fields.name: api
fields.doc: What to call instead of Tauri's API (a fake window or `invoke` in a test).

files.about:
The zoom of the page, as a program has it: Ctrl with + or = (in), - (out) and 0 (back to 100%), or Ctrl and the
wheel, from 50% to 200% in steps of 10% (WCAG 1.4.4 asks for 200%). Tauri leaves the engine's own zoom keys off
(`zoomHotkeysEnabled`), so the page does it and gives the level to the webview (`setZoom`). On a Mac, Command takes
the place of Ctrl for the keys.
The level is kept in the webview's `localStorage`, which is the app's on that machine, and set again at the next
start. A level the webview refuses goes back to the last one it took, and is not kept.
A key or a wheel whose default a part of the page already took (a canvas that zooms itself) is left to that part.
`createZoom` is the controller without React (the settings of an app share it with the keys); `useZoom` puts it on
the document for as long as a component is mounted and gives the level to show.

types.name: UseZoomOptions
types.doc: The options of `useZoom`: those of `createZoom`, and whether it acts. The level comes back from the hook.

fields.name: enabled
fields.doc: Default: in a window of its own (`readHost().ownWindow`), or when `api` is given.

fields.name: onError
fields.doc: Where a refused or failed `setZoom` goes.

fields.name: storageKey
fields.doc: Where the level is kept. Default `sigrid.zoom`; an app gives its own to keep a level it already saved.

fields.name: storage
fields.doc: Default: the page's `localStorage`. `null` keeps nothing.

fields.name: api
fields.doc: What to call instead of Tauri's API (a fake webview in a test).

types.name: ZoomController
types.doc: One zoom for the page: the keys, the wheel and an app's own control share it.

fields.name: ready
fields.doc: Settles when the saved level was given to the webview (or refused, and the level is back at 100%).

fields.name: level
fields.doc: The level shown now: 1 is 100%.

fields.name: set
fields.doc: Shows `level` at once and resolves to whether the webview took it.

fields.name: step
fields.doc: One step: 1 in, -1 out, 0 back to 100%.

fields.name: attach
fields.doc: Takes the zoom keys and Ctrl with the wheel on `doc`; returns the function that lets them go.

types.name: ZoomKey
types.doc: What `zoomKey` reads of a key.

fields.name: storageKey
fields.doc: Where the level is kept. Default `sigrid.zoom`; an app gives its own to keep a level it already saved.

fields.name: storage
fields.doc: Default: the page's `localStorage`. `null` keeps nothing.

fields.name: onError
